syllabus.clause: a successful write is not durable. Durability may need both the file data AND the directory metadata on stable storage: fsync the file and its parent directory after create or rename, and use the write-temp + fsync + rename + fsync-dir atomic-replace pattern. In Rust, File::sync_all vs sync_data. After fsyncgate (PostgreSQL, 2018), a failed fsync may drop dirty pages, so retrying can lie; crash and recover from the WAL instead (Rebello et al., USENIX ATC 2020). Torn writes and RWF_ATOMIC (Linux 6.11+, direct I/O, needs hardware support).

items.item: The atomic-replace example's reset step (going back from the long content to the short content) is implemented with the exact same write-temp-fsync-rename sequence as the forward step, not a plain overwrite, because an early draft of this example used a plain overwrite for the reset and it produced real partial reads — the bug was in the test's own reset step, not in the atomic-replace pattern, and that finding is itself evidence for why the full sequence matters everywhere, not just on the interesting half.

items.item: The fsyncgate incident's lesson is not that fsync is unreliable in general; it is that a single failure permanently changes what a subsequent retry can observe, because the file system's own internal bookkeeping (the dirty bit) was already updated by the failed attempt, which is a specific, narrow claim quite different from a vague warning that fsync 'can fail'.
